summary: Suggests an X.500 Directory Schema, or naming architecture, for use in the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4524.

eli5.summary: It is a plan for what kinds of entries a directory should hold and how to name them.

subtitle: A shared X.500 directory schema for the COSINE and Internet pilots, plus a process for growing it.

tldr.problem: The X.500 standard gave only a basis for a directory schema, so pilot directories would each define the same extra object classes and attributes privately and remote systems could not tell what they meant.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a shared set of pilot object classes and attribute types, a conformance statement for directory servers and user agents, and proforma-based procedures to add and retire definitions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1274 was a Proposed Standard and has since been obsoleted by RFC 4524.

today: RFC 1274 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4524, which is the document to use now.

sections.title: Why a Shared Schema
sections.content:
The 1988 CCITT X.500 / ISO IS9594 recommendations standardised Directory Services. They define useful object classes (in X.521) and attribute types (in X.520), but the memo says these are insufficient as a basis for a large scale pilot directory.

If administrators define their own extras, the same objects and attribute types get privately defined many times over, and remote systems cannot determine what they mean. This memo grows out of its forerunner, the THORN and RARE Naming Architecture, whose definitions were heavily used in early pilots and by the THORN and Quipu implementations.

Because requirements keep growing, the schema is treated as a living document. Esoteric or highly experimental needs should stay private, requirements backed by more than one site will usually be integrated, and duplication for similar real world objects will be avoided.
sections.eli5: If every school made up its own names for things in the phone book, nobody could read anyone else's book. A shared list of names fixes that.

sections.title: What Conformance Means
sections.content:
A system claiming conformance has minimum duties. A Directory System Agent (DSA) shall be able to store all the attributes and object class values specified, which implies support for what X.509 strong authentication needs. A Directory User Agent (DUA) shall be able to identify each attribute type and object class to the user, for example as a string.

Both statements are qualified for large attribute values (over 1 kbyte): a DSA need not store them and a DUA need not display them, though it must indicate their presence.

Desirable but not required: matching correctly on all defined syntaxes, enforcing the implied object class schema, displaying all syntaxes correctly, and keeping compatibility with a previous version of the schema.
sections.eli5: A directory that follows the plan must at least keep every kind of entry and be able to say what each kind is called. Doing fancier things is nice but optional.

sections.title: Adding and Retiring Definitions
sections.content:
New object classes and attribute types are requested by mailing completed proformas to the schema editor. An object class proforma has three fields (Object Class, Description, ASN1OCMacro). An attribute type proforma has five (Attribute Type, Description, OCMust, OCMay, ASN1ATMacro). The memo's examples use a made-up 'alcoholic drink' class and a 'hue' attribute.

Changing an existing object class by adding optional attributes will be granted. A change that alters the mandatory attributes will not be: a new object class is created and the original is expired. Someone unhappy with an editorial decision can raise it on the osi-ds mailing list.

Large groups can be integrated in two ways: moving well-structured, widely used private definitions into the schema, or allocating a subtree, with the pilotGroups object identifier defined for this. Old definitions are retired gracefully: the intent is announced on the list, and absent objections the definition is marked with an expiry date and stays in the schema until then. Users may argue for retention.
sections.eli5: To add a new kind of entry you fill in a form. Old kinds are not thrown away suddenly; people get a warning and a date first.

sections.title: Pilot Object Classes and Identifiers
sections.content:
The schema supports the standard X.500 and X.400 object classes and adds COSINE/Internet ones. Examples include pilotObject, a subclass of top that lets common attributes such as info, photo, manager and lastModifiedTime be attached to entries of any class, and pilotPerson, a subclass of person adding attributes such as userid, rfc822Mailbox and roomNumber.

Others cover accounts, documents, rooms, document series, DNS and other domains, a domain related object, friendly country, a simple security object, pilot organization, pilot DSA and quality labelled data.

The memo anchors its object identifiers under pilot, which is {ucl 100}, with sub-branches for attribute types (1), attribute syntaxes (3), object classes (4) and groups (10).
sections.eli5: The memo lists ready-made kinds of entries, like person, room, document and organisation, each with a list of facts you can store about it.

sections.title: Attribute Types and Syntaxes
sections.content:
Section 9 defines a long list of COSINE/Internet attribute types, from userid, rfc822Mailbox and favouriteDrink to document fields, telephone numbers, DNS record types (MX, NS, SOA, CNAME), associatedDomain, quality attributes for DSAs, personalSignature and audio.

It also lists generally useful syntaxes and a table of upper bounds on the length of attribute values. Appendices give the proforma in BNF, tools to check proformas, and the full schema in ASN.1 macro format so that system schema tables can be derived by machine.
sections.eli5: Each kind of entry can hold labelled facts, like an email address or a phone number, and the memo lists the labels and how long each can be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that security issues are not discussed in it. It does say that a conforming server must support the object classes and attribute types needed for X.509 strong authentication.
sections.eli5: The memo does not cover security itself, apart from saying servers must be able to store the entries needed for strong login checks.
